labs.fennick: Morning cortisol and ACTH are suppressed during ongoing prednisone exposure.
labs.hint: Suppression during exogenous glucocorticoid use reflects HPA-axis suppression; it is not a screen for a hidden cortisol-producing tumor.

labs.name: Vitamin D
labs.result: 25-hydroxy vitamin D is low.
labs.remark: At least that one has a straightforward supplement.
labs.fennick: 25-hydroxy vitamin D is below range.
labs.hint: Replace the deficiency as part of bone protection, alongside calcium intake and fracture-risk assessment.

labs.name: Urinalysis
labs.result: No glucose, protein, blood, or evidence of infection.
labs.remark: One section of the chart can stay uncomplicated.
labs.fennick: Urinalysis is unremarkable.
labs.hint: This does not explain the phenotype. The medication history remains the highest-yield evidence.

management.title: Identify the cause without unnecessary testing
management.hint: When the phenotype and a sustained supraphysiologic glucocorticoid exposure already align, confirm the medication history before ordering a search for an endogenous source.
management.hintPatient: The answer may be in the prescription list rather than a scanner.
management.prompt: He takes prednisone 20 mg daily and has a classic Cushing phenotype. What is the best next diagnostic step?
management.promptRemark: I can make time for one sensible plan. I cannot make time for every scanner in the building.
management.fennick: Document total glucocorticoid exposure and why it was prescribed. Do not launch an endogenous Cushing workup while the exogenous cause is clear.
management.quote: A diagnosis from the history. That is unexpectedly efficient.

options.text: Confirm the complete glucocorticoid exposure and its indication
options.feedback: Correct. A sustained supraphysiologic glucocorticoid exposure plus the phenotype establishes the exogenous source. Document the full exposure and indication before ordering endocrine imaging or screening that prednisone will confound.
options.patientCorrect: Then put the prednisone at the top of the chart this time.

options.text: Order pituitary MRI to search for an ACTH-secreting lesion
options.feedback: Pituitary imaging is for established ACTH-dependent endogenous Cushing disease, not an obvious exogenous presentation.
options.patientWrong: Another imaging order? The prednisone is already sitting on the medication list.
options.fennWrong: Pituitary imaging follows biochemical evidence of ACTH-dependent endogenous disease, which is not established here.

options.text: Perform overnight dexamethasone suppression testing while he continues prednisone
options.feedback: Exogenous glucocorticoids interfere with HPA physiology and testing. The medication history already explains the syndrome.
options.patientWrong: A test the medication interferes with will not improve this meeting.
options.fennWrong: Prednisone distorts HPA physiology, so a suppression test now cannot answer the intended question.

options.text: Order adrenal CT for an autonomous cortisol-producing mass
options.feedback: Imaging risks incidental findings and does not supersede the clear exogenous exposure.
options.patientWrong: Scanning every gland still sounds like avoiding the prescription list.
options.fennWrong: Adrenal imaging now risks an incidentaloma while ignoring the documented exposure.

management.openingFenn: The exposure is already documented. Do not let an incidental finding replace it.

management.title: Reduce glucocorticoids safely
management.hint: Remove the unnecessary exposure without provoking adrenal insufficiency: larger reductions are tolerated at high doses, then the taper slows near physiologic dosing.
management.hintPatient: I want fewer tablets, but not a new emergency.
management.prompt: The original pain condition is stable and prednisone is no longer justified. How should it be stopped?
management.promptRemark: If the medicine caused this, I would prefer not to take tomorrow morning.
management.fennick: Not abruptly. Taper toward physiologic dosing, monitor symptoms, and reassess the underlying condition throughout.
management.quote: A controlled exit rather than a dramatic one. Fine.

options.text: Use a monitored taper that slows near physiologic dosing
options.feedback: Correct. Taper only after the underlying condition is controlled, with larger reductions tolerated at high doses and slower reductions near physiologic dosing. Monitor for recurrence, withdrawal, and adrenal insufficiency throughout.
options.patientCorrect: Put it on a calendar and I will follow it.

options.text: Stop prednisone immediately and monitor symptoms as needed
options.feedback: Abrupt cessation after prolonged use risks glucocorticoid withdrawal and adrenal insufficiency or crisis.
options.patientWrong: I wanted fewer tablets, not a collapse tomorrow morning.
options.fennWrong: Abrupt withdrawal after prolonged use can precipitate adrenal insufficiency or crisis.

options.text: Continue prednisone indefinitely and add ketoconazole
options.feedback: The cortisol-like exposure is the prednisone itself. Blocking endogenous synthesis while continuing the unnecessary drug is not appropriate.
options.patientWrong: That adds a medicine while preserving the one that caused the problem.
options.fennWrong: Continuing the causal drug while blocking endogenous synthesis does not remove the exposure.

options.text: Arrange bilateral adrenalectomy to eliminate cortisol production
options.feedback: His adrenal glands are suppressed, not the source of excess. Surgery is not indicated.
options.patientWrong: Removing quiet glands is not a controlled taper.
options.fennWrong: The adrenal glands are suppressed rather than surgically overactive.

management.openingFenn: Long exposure means the exit must be controlled, not abrupt.

management.title: Prevent and treat complications
management.hint: Think beyond appearance: cardiovascular risk, glucose, bone, infection, vitamin status, and adrenal safety all need a place in follow-up.
management.hintPatient: The taper does not undo eighteen months of effects by itself.
management.prompt: What belongs in the follow-up plan?
management.promptRemark: I would like the entire consequence list, even the inconvenient parts.
management.fennick: Blood pressure, glucose, bone health, infection risk, lipids, potassium, and eye symptoms all deserve active review.
management.quote: That is a longer list than the original prescription came with.

options.text: Treat metabolic and bone complications and provide steroid-safety education
options.feedback: Correct. Treat blood pressure, dysglycaemia, lipids, potassium, bone loss, vitamin deficiency, infection risk, and ocular symptoms while exposure is reduced. Bone and cardiovascular protection should not wait for taper completion.
options.patientCorrect: Give me the monitoring schedule as well as the taper.

options.text: Focus follow-up on weight reduction and cosmetic recovery
options.feedback: The major risks are systemic: diabetes, hypertension, osteoporosis, infection, thrombosis, and adrenal suppression.
options.patientWrong: The bruises and weak legs are not a weight-loss discussion.
options.fennWrong: The dangerous consequences are metabolic, skeletal, infectious, cardiovascular, and adrenal—not merely cosmetic.

options.text: Wait until the taper is complete before addressing hypertension or dysglycemia
options.feedback: Complications should be treated now while glucocorticoid exposure is reduced.
options.patientWrong: My calendar can hold two plans at once. Start the monitoring now.
options.fennWrong: Hypertension and dysglycaemia require treatment during the taper, not after it.

options.text: Recommend bariatric surgery before correcting the glucocorticoid exposure
options.feedback: The body-composition change is medication-driven. Treat the cause and metabolic risks before considering unrelated surgery.
options.patientWrong: I would rather remove the cause than schedule unrelated surgery.
options.fennWrong: Surgery does not address medication-driven body composition or the underlying risks.

management.openingFenn: The taper is only one part; treat the complications already present.

management.title: Prepare him for the taper
management.hint: A safe plan is one the patient can follow during ordinary days and illness: written dosing, sick-day rules, warning symptoms, and shared decisions.
management.hintPatient: Give me a plan I can understand when I am tired or unwell.
management.prompt: What should he understand before leaving?
management.promptRemark: What would make this plan fail?
management.fennick: Explain withdrawal and adrenal-insufficiency symptoms, sick-day guidance, and when urgent evaluation is needed.
management.quote: Clear thresholds. That I can work with.

options.text: Give a written taper, sick-day rules, and adrenal warning signs
options.feedback: Correct. Provide a written taper, sick-day instructions, warning symptoms, and clear thresholds for urgent care. Shared decisions and coordinated follow-up reduce unsafe self-adjustment.
options.patientCorrect: Written, specific, and without blame. Good.

options.text: Tell him only to take fewer tablets and call if concerned
options.feedback: A vague plan invites dosing errors and misses essential adrenal-safety education.
options.patientWrong: “Take fewer” is not a schedule I can follow.
options.fennWrong: A vague instruction invites dosing errors and omits adrenal-safety guidance.

options.text: Emphasize that taking prednisone was irresponsible
options.feedback: Blame does not improve safety. He followed repeated prescriptions; focus on informed future decisions and coordinated care.
options.patientWrong: I came for a safe plan, not a verdict on trusting my doctors.
options.fennWrong: Blame adds no safety information; he followed repeatedly renewed prescriptions.

options.text: Promise his appearance and strength will normalize within one week
options.feedback: Recovery of HPA function and Cushing features is variable and often takes months. Avoid false certainty.
options.patientWrong: Do not promise a one-week repair for an eighteen-month problem.
options.fennWrong: Recovery of strength, appearance, and HPA function is variable and often slow.

management.openingFenn: Give him a written plan that still works on a sick day.

hints.fenn: The phenotype says glucocorticoid excess. The medication history tells you whether it came from inside or outside the body.
hints.patient: The prednisone is probably more relevant than my schedule.

hints.fenn: Exogenous Cushing syndrome does not require pituitary and adrenal imaging when the exposure is clear.
hints.patient: No gland hunt. Understood.

hints.fenn: Long-term prednisone suppresses the HPA axis; stopping abruptly can be dangerous.
hints.patient: So “stop the cause” still requires a taper.

hints.fenn: The case is not over at the taper: glucose, blood pressure, bone, infection, and adrenal safety all matter.
hints.patient: I need a follow-up plan, not merely fewer tablets.

debrief.title: Iatrogenic Cushing Syndrome
debrief.pearl: A complete medication history is the key diagnostic test for exogenous Cushing syndrome. If long-term glucocorticoids are no longer needed, taper them rather than stopping abruptly, usually slowing near physiologic doses, and actively address metabolic, cardiovascular, skeletal, infectious, and adrenal-safety consequences.
